P2E00.d: Gear lever position sensor A is the first of up to four sensors through which an electronic selector tells its control module where the lever sits. In the designs GM and Toyota document, A and B form a redundant pair that each report the full lever position; GM's patent US9249877 has each of its two sensors deliver an x and a y value.
s: Warning lamp or shift-system message
Gear selection still possible through sensor B, sometimes delayed
With a second fault, the vehicle may stay in P or N
c: Loose connector or chafed wire at the selector assembly
Supply or ground of sensor A interrupted
Sensor A inside the selector assembly failed
Input stage of the evaluating module faulty

P2E01.d: Here sensor A of the gear lever delivers values that are electrically valid but not believable. Two makers document the code.
s: MIL on after two trips
Shift-system message, selector still works through sensor B
Often no noticeable driving difference
c: Selector logic needs a software update (Lexus NX 2022–24)
Sensor A reports an internal error
Magnet or lever mechanism shifted, so sensor A reads off the gate

P2E02.d: P2E02 says the signal of gear lever position sensor A is stuck below the lowest value a healthy sensor can output. Typical reasons: the signal wire touches ground, the reference voltage is missing, or the sensor output has collapsed.
s: Warning lamp and shift-system message
Lever position shown on the display jumps or is missing
If sensor B also fails, no range can be selected
c: Signal wire of sensor A shorted to ground
Sensor reference voltage missing or pulled down

P2E03.d: With P2E03 the module sees the signal of sensor A above the highest value the sensor can legitimately send. On a pulled-up input this happens when the signal wire is open; it also follows a short to the supply or a lost sensor ground.
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Shift-system message, ranges still selectable via sensor B
Start or range change refused if both sensors are affected
c: Signal wire of sensor A open at a connector
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage

P2E04.d: Sensor B is the second, redundant gear lever position sensor; it measures the same lever travel as sensor A so that a single failure does not leave the driver without range selection. Toyota names it gear lever position sensor B in the floor shift assembly of the Lexus NX, and GM's tables call the equivalent device sensor 2, with X and Y values of its own (P089B to P08A2).
s: Warning lamp or shift-system message
Selector works normally on sensor A alone
Any further sensor fault can block range changes
c: Connector or wire of sensor B at the selector loose or damaged
Sensor B in the selector assembly failed
Separate supply branch of sensor B interrupted

P2E05.d: P2E05 flags implausible data from sensor B, the backup gear lever sensor. It is one of the few codes of this family with public manufacturer use.
s: MIL on, usually without a driveability change
Shift-system warning may appear and disappear
Often stored together with P2E01
c: Floor shift assembly logic outdated (Lexus NX bulletin L-SB-0050-22)
Sensor B signals an internal error
Sensor B or its magnet misaligned after a repair in the console

P2E06.d: The signal of sensor B, the redundant gear lever sensor, has dropped under its permitted minimum. Electrically that points to a short to ground in its signal line, a dead sensor or a missing feed on its own supply branch.
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Selector keeps working on sensor A
Range selection lost if sensor A fails as well
c: Signal line of sensor B shorted to ground
Supply branch of sensor B dead

P2E07.d: P2E07 is the high-side circuit fault of gear lever position sensor B: its signal reads above anything the sensor may legitimately produce. An interrupted signal line on an input with pull-up, a short to battery or reference voltage, or a broken sensor ground are the classic causes.
s: Warning lamp and shift-system message
Normal shifting via sensor A
With P2E03 present as well, range selection may be blocked
c: Signal line of sensor B open
Signal line shorted to battery or reference voltage

P2E08.d: A third gear lever position sensor, C, only exists on selectors with more than the usual redundant pair. Toyota's patent US10180184 shows such a design: four Hall sensors in a row face a magnet in the shift lever, the voltages they produce encode the position, and if any one of them is faulty the other three still allow limp-home driving.
s: Warning lamp or shift-system message
Shifting continues on the remaining sensors
A further sensor fault may force neutral
c: Connector or wiring at the selector assembly faulty
Sensor C inside the selector failed

P2E09.d: P2E09 means sensor C produces an electrically valid signal that contradicts the lever position given by the other sensors. No manufacturer documents this code or names the role of a sensor C, so the logic can only be inferred from the component.
s: Warning appears only after certain lever movements
Range display briefly disagrees with lever position
Limp-home with restricted selection possible
c: Sensor C output frozen at an intermediate value
Magnet or lever mechanism worn or displaced
Plausibility logic of the selector software too strict

P2E0A.d: For P2E0A the module reads the signal of gear lever sensor C below the window a working sensor can occupy. On a voltage-output Hall sensor like those in Toyota's four-sensor selector patent (US10180184), this means a signal line pulled to ground, a missing feed or a sensor that has stopped driving its output.
s: Warning lamp or shift message
Limp-home on the remaining sensors
No noticeable change while other sensors are valid
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground

P2E0B.d: P2E0B: sensor C of the gear lever reports more than its maximum valid signal. That is the typical picture of a broken signal wire on a pulled-up input, contact with the feed line or a lost sensor ground.
s: Warning lamp or shift message
Selector keeps working with the other sensors
Neutral forced if another sensor also fails
c: Signal wire of sensor C open
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage

P2E0C.d: Sensor D is the fourth and last letter in this family of gear lever position sensors. A layout that needs four is described in Toyota's patent US10180184: four Hall sensors lined up along the shift direction under one magnet, whose voltage pattern flips when the lever moves sideways, so both shift and select movement can be read.
s: Warning lamp or shift-system message
Gear selection usually still works
Neutral fail-safe possible after a second sensor fault
c: Selector connector or wiring of sensor D faulty
Module input for sensor D faulty

P2E0D.d: With P2E0D the fourth lever sensor, D, stays within its electrical limits but its reading does not fit the lever position. No manufacturer documents P2E0D.
s: Code appears only after selecting a certain position
Warning lamp or shift message
Limp-home with fewer sensors
c: Sensor D frozen at a middle value
Magnet position in the lever changed by wear or impact
Selector software tolerance needs an update

P2E0E.d: P2E0E is set when the output of gear lever position sensor D drops beneath its lowest plausible level, usually near 0 V or 0 % duty cycle. Likely reasons are a ground short in the D signal path, a sensor without feed or a Hall element whose output died.
s: Shift-system warning
Selector still usable on the other sensors
Shift to neutral if another sensor fails
c: Signal path of sensor D shorted to ground
Hall element of sensor D failed low

P2E0F.d: P2E0F closes the series: sensor D, the fourth gear lever position sensor, reads above the top of its valid range. An open signal wire where the module input pulls up, contact with a voltage-carrying wire or a lost sensor ground produce this picture.
s: Warning lamp or shift message
Normal shifting on the remaining sensors
Neutral fail-safe after a further fault
c: Signal wire of sensor D open
Signal wire touching a voltage-carrying wire

P2E10.d: P2E10 is the general circuit code for the sensor reporting where the gear selection actuator stands, the motor-driven unit that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual or dual-clutch gearbox to the wanted gear or gate. The control module stores it when signal or supply of that sensor are electrically faulty in a way the dedicated low, high or erratic codes do not cover.
s: Transmission warning and MIL
Gearbox holds one gear or goes to neutral (limp mode)
Shifts refused or engaging drive or reverse not possible
c: Corroded or loose connector, damaged harness at the actuator
Position sensor in the actuator failed (often only replaceable with the actuator)
Sensor reference voltage missing or loaded down by another fault
Input stage in the transmission control module faulty

P2E11.d: With P2E11 the position sensor of the gear selection actuator delivers values that are electrically fine but do not fit the situation: the reading stays put although the actuator was driven, or it contradicts the gear that shaft speeds prove to be engaged. No manufacturer documents P2E11 publicly.
s: Delayed or harsh shifts, gear sometimes not engaged
Transmission warning, possibly limp mode with fixed gear
Fault may clear after a relearn procedure
c: Learned end positions lost or outdated, e.g. after battery disconnect or part replacement
Sensor magnet or sensor mounting shifted, reading offset
Wear or binding in the selection mechanism, actuator does not reach its target

P2E12.d: P2E12 sets when the signal of the gear selection actuator's position sensor stays below the lowest valid level. Usual reasons are a short to ground on the signal line, a missing 5 V reference or a defect inside the sensor; with many designs an interrupted signal wire also reads low.
s: MIL and transmission warning immediately
Limp mode, no gear changes or only one gear
Further sensor codes if the shared 5 V supply is affected
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference missing or pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Internal short in the position sensor

P2E13.d: P2E13 is the opposite case to P2E12: the position signal of the gear selection actuator sits above its highest plausible value. A short between the signal line and a supply wire is the classic cause; an open ground or, on pull-up inputs, a broken signal wire produce the same picture.
s: MIL and transmission warning
Gearbox stays in one gear or in neutral
Shift lever input ignored
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply or 5 V reference line
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Position sensor faulty, output stuck high
Moisture in the actuator connector bridging pins

P2E14.d: P2E14 covers a position signal from the gear selection actuator that is present but unsteady: it drops out for moments, jumps or carries an implausible frequency or pattern, without staying low or high long enough for P2E12 or P2E13. No manufacturer documents P2E14 publicly.
s: Occasional refused or delayed shifts
Short drops to neutral while driving
Warning lamp that comes and goes
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the actuator connector
Harness chafing that only shorts or opens under vibration or heat
Interference from damaged shielding or nearby motor wiring
Sensor with an internal intermittent fault

P2E15.d: P2E15 is the basic circuit code for the position sensor of a second selection actuator, one assigned to the intermediate shaft (layshaft) of the gearbox rather than to the main gear selection, which has P2E10 to P2E14. Which gearboxes use such an actuator, and what exactly it engages there, no manufacturer documents publicly for this code.
s: Transmission warning and MIL
Some gears unavailable or gearbox in limp mode
Vehicle may only drive in a restricted range of gears
c: Connector or harness to the intermediate shaft actuator damaged or corroded
Position sensor of the actuator failed
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module

P2E16.d: P2E16 flags a position reading from the intermediate shaft selection actuator that is electrically valid but not credible, for example a travel that does not match the commanded movement or the learned end stops. No manufacturer documents P2E16 publicly.
s: Harsh, slow or failed shifts involving the intermediate shaft
Transmission warning, possibly limp mode
Fault returns until a relearn has been done
c: End stops not learned or lost after battery disconnect or repair
Actuator or selection linkage binding, target position not reached
Sensor or its magnet shifted, reading offset

P2E17.d: P2E17 tells you the position signal of the intermediate shaft selection actuator is stuck at the bottom of its range or below it. On the bench this usually turns out to be a signal line touching ground, a dead reference supply, or a sensor whose output stage has failed.
s: MIL and transmission warning
Limp mode with limited gears
Code returns at once after clearing
c: Output stage of the position sensor failed
Signal wire interrupted (on sensors that then read low)

P2E18.d: Here the position sensor of the intermediate shaft selection actuator reports a value above its upper limit. Most often the signal line has contact with battery voltage or the 5 V feed, or the sensor has lost its ground so the output floats upward.
s: MIL and transmission warning
Certain gears blocked, limp mode
Poor acceleration because the gearbox holds an unsuitable gear
c: Signal line shorted to battery voltage or the 5 V feed
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module

P2E19.d: P2E19 is stored when the intermediate shaft selection actuator's position sensor delivers a signal that flickers, drops out briefly or changes faster than the mechanism could physically move. Because the fault comes and goes, the code often shows as pending or with only a few occurrences.
s: Sporadic shift faults that disappear again
Warning lamp only now and then
Short limp-mode episodes
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the actuator or gearbox connector
Harness rubbing on the housing, contact only under vibration
Sensor with an internal intermittent fault

P2E1A.d: P2E1A sets when the two DC voltage readings inside the drive motor A inverter, sensor A and sensor B, stop agreeing although they should describe the same high-voltage potential. Each value may pass its own range test; the fault lies in the mismatch.
s: Hybrid system or drive warning lamp, MIL possible
Reduced or no electric drive power
Further inverter voltage codes stored at the same time
c: One of the two voltage measuring channels in the inverter has drifted
Fault in the inverter or power drive unit electronics
Poor high-voltage connection between the two measuring points
Control software with an unsuitable comparison window

P2E1B.d: P2E1B reports an electrical fault in the circuit of the phase X current sensor of drive motor A, without a separate low or high verdict. X, Y and Z name a second three-phase winding group: a Mitsubishi Electric patent on two-group motors for hybrid drives couples one current sensor to the conductor of each of the six phases.
s: Hybrid system warning lamp and MIL
Reduced electric drive or no electric drive
Rough or noisy motor operation under load
c: Phase X current sensor in the inverter failed
Reference supply or ground of the current sensors faulty
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Defect on the motor control board that evaluates the sensor

P2E1C.d: P2E1C means the phase X current sensor of drive motor A delivers a value that is electrically valid but implausible. No manufacturer documents P2E1C publicly; GM's U/V/W counterparts show the usual test, a zero check.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited, uneven torque at low speed
Code returns after clearing at the next start
c: Zero offset of the phase X sensor has drifted
Sensor gain error after ageing or overheating
Unstable reference voltage for the current sensors
Fault in the measuring stage of the inverter control board

P2E1D.d: P2E1D says the phase X current sensor signal of drive motor A lies below its lowest valid value. Phase current flows in both directions, so the sensor reports a signed quantity; low therefore means a reading more negative than any real current, not a weak current.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Sharp loss of electric drive power
Vehicle may only drive in a reduced mode
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground inside the inverter
Supply voltage of the phase X sensor missing

P2E1E.d: P2E1E flags a phase X current sensor signal of drive motor A above the top of its valid range. No manufacturer documents P2E1E publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive cut off or strongly limited
Possible jolt when the inverter shuts down
c: Sensor signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase X current sensor
Phase X current sensor failed high

P2E1F.d: P2E1F stands for a circuit fault of the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A that is not sorted into a low or high case. No manufacturer documents P2E1F publicly, and even the U/V/W equivalents of this general code see little use: GM's 2013 to 2019 hybrid tables cover the phase sensors with offset, low, high and sum checks only, while Ford's 2019 hybrid summary says that current sensor faults of its motor inverter
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited or switched off
Other phase current codes may be stored as well
c: Phase Y current sensor in the inverter failed
Poor contact at the inverter's low-voltage connector

P2E20.d: P2E20 is set when the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A reads within its electrical limits but not believably. No manufacturer documents P2E20 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Less electric assist, torque not as requested
Motor whine or slight vibration
c: Gain error of the phase Y sensor
Zero offset of the phase Y sensor shifted
Disturbed reference voltage of the current sensors
Motor control software needing an update

P2E21.d: P2E21 records that the phase Y current sensor of drive motor A reports a value under the bottom of its scale. No manufacturer documents P2E21 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited
Engine runs more often than usual on hybrids
c: Phase Y sensor signal shorted to ground

P2E22.d: P2E22 is stored when the phase Y current sensor signal of drive motor A sticks above its upper limit. No manufacturer documents P2E22 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive switched off or strongly limited
High codes of other phases stored at the same time
c: Phase Y signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase Y sensor
Shared sensor reference faulty, other phases affected too

P2E23.d: P2E23 points to a wiring or circuit defect around the phase Z current sensor of drive motor A that is not classed as low or high. Whether a Z sensor exists at all depends on the design.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited or switched off
Fault may come and go with vibration or temperature
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Phase Z current sensor in the inverter failed
Supply or ground of the Z sensor interrupted

P2E24.d: P2E24 concerns a phase Z current reading of drive motor A that passes the electrical checks yet fails a plausibility test. No manufacturer documents P2E24 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited
Uneven torque or motor noise
c: Zero offset of the phase Z sensor drifted
Gain error of the phase Z sensor
Faulty measuring stage on the inverter control board

P2E25.d: P2E25 means the phase Z current sensor of drive motor A reports below its valid minimum. No manufacturer documents P2E25 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Reduced electric drive
Low codes of other phases possibly stored too
c: Phase Z sensor signal shorted to ground
Shared sensor reference or ground faulty

P2E26.d: P2E26 reports a phase Z current sensor signal of drive motor A that sits above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2E26 publicly.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive torque clearly reduced
Vehicle continues only in a reduced-power mode
c: Phase Z signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase Z sensor
Phase Z current sensor failed high

P2E27.d: P2E27 compares the three current sensors of phases X, Y and Z of drive motor A with each other. Mitsubishi Electric's patent joins the X, Y and Z windings in a star, so their currents must add up to almost zero at every instant; a clear residual means at least one sensor is wrong, even if every reading passes its own checks.
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited or temporarily switched off
No single sensor code stored alongside
c: One of the three X/Y/Z sensors drifted in offset or gain
Disturbed common reference of the current sensors
Leakage current from the X/Y/Z winding group to the housing

P2E28.d: P2E28 concerns a drive motor with an electrically excited rotor, the type Nissan uses in the Ariya and BMW in its fifth-generation eDrive. Such a rotor carries a field coil that receives direct current through brushes and slip rings; a sensor measures that current for the closed field-control loop.
s: Electric drive warning or service message
Noticeably reduced drive power
Vehicle may refuse to drive or stop driving
c: Excitation current sensor drifted (offset or gain no longer correct)
Faulty excitation power stage, so actual and expected current differ
Worn brushes or dirty slip rings changing the field circuit resistance
Inverter or motor control software fault

P2E29.d: P2E29 reports that the signal voltage of the excitation current sensor of drive motor A has dropped below the band the controller accepts. The sensor sits in the excitation stage that feeds direct current to the rotor field coil of an electrically excited motor; TI names shunts with isolated amplifiers or isolated Hall-effect sensors for this job.
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed

P2E2A.d: P2E2A is the counterpart to P2E29: the signal from the sensor that measures the rotor field current of drive motor A sits above the highest voltage a working sensor can deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply rail, an open ground or reference connection that lets the input float up, or a failed sensor output stage.
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Reduced or no drive power
Fault returns immediately after clearing
c: Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor ground or reference connection

P2E2B.d: P2E2B does not blame the sensor: the measured field current of drive motor A itself exceeds what the controller allows. In TI's example of an excitation stage, two switches and two diodes sit between the high-voltage rails; with both switches on, the rotor coil sees the entire DC-link voltage, and switches of this kind are rarely sized above about 50 A.
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Sudden loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not restart the drive system
c: Excitation power switch shorted or stuck on
Field current control or gate driver fault in the inverter
Shorted turns in the rotor field winding

P2E2C.d: P2E2C covers the low-voltage supply that powers the control electronics of on-board charger A, not the AC input. The code means this supply voltage is present but behaves implausibly, for example it fluctuates or disagrees with what other modules see on the same 12 V network.
s: Plug-in charging does not start or stops early
Charging system warning message
Fault comes and goes with electrical load or vibration
c: Loose or corroded supply or ground connection at the charger
Ground offset between charger and other modules
Unstable 12 V supply from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module

P2E2D.d: P2E2D is set when the 12 V feed of the control board in on-board charger A stays below its lower limit. The usual suspects sit outside the charger: a discharged or failing 12 V battery, a DC/DC converter that is not keeping the network up, a blown fuse in the feed, or resistance in supply or ground wiring that eats voltage under load.
s: Plug-in charging refused or interrupted
Further low-voltage faults in other modules
Charging status display behaves erratically
c: Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger supply
High resistance in supply or ground wiring
DC/DC converter not maintaining the 12 V network

P2E2E.d: P2E2E reports the opposite of P2E2D: the low-voltage feed of on-board charger A rises above its upper limit. On a plug-in vehicle the 12 V network is held by the DC/DC converter, so a converter regulating too high is the first suspect; an external charger or jump-start device at excessive voltage can do the same, and a faulty measurement inside the charger can fake the reading.
s: Plug-in charging stops or will not start
Overvoltage faults stored in other modules as well
Lamps unusually bright or 12 V battery overcharged
c: DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
External battery charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module

P2E2F.d: P2E2F concerns the 12 V feed of the control electronics in a second on-board charger, charger B, not its grid input. The voltage is within limits but behaves implausibly, for example it jumps around or disagrees with the system voltage that other modules report.
s: Plug-in charging starts late, pauses or stops
Fault appears with electrical load changes or vibration
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
c: Loose or corroded supply or ground terminal at charger B
Ground offset between charger B and the reference module
Fluctuating 12 V network from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B

P2E30.d: P2E30 is stored when the 12 V feed reaching the control board of charger B stays under its lower limit. Most causes lie upstream: a flat or aged 12 V battery, a blown fuse or failed relay in the charger feed, or corroded supply and ground contacts that lose voltage under load.
s: Charging through charger B does not start
Low-voltage or communication faults in other modules too
Reduced charging power if only one charger works
c: Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger B feed
Voltage drop across corroded supply or ground contacts
DC/DC converter not holding up the 12 V network

P2E31.d: P2E31 is the high-side counterpart of P2E30: the low-voltage feed of charger B climbs above what its control electronics accept. On plug-in cars the DC/DC converter holds the 12 V network, so a converter regulating too high is the main suspect; a workshop charger or jump pack set too high, or a faulty measurement inside charger B, can give the same reading.
s: Charging via charger B stops or will not start
Overvoltage codes stored in several modules
12 V battery gassing or lamps unusually bright
c: DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
Workshop charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B

P2E32.d: P2E32 belongs to the forced shutdown input of on-board charger A, a hardwired signal with which another module can switch the charger off regardless of bus messages. The code means this signal does not behave as expected although its level is in range, for instance the charger keeps converting power after a shutdown request, or the line reports shutdown while none was commanded.
s: Plug-in charging refused or ended unexpectedly
Charging system warning message
c: Contact resistance or partly corroded terminal in the shutdown line
Shutdown input stage inside charger A not responding correctly
Fault or software issue in the module driving the shutdown signal

P2E33.d: P2E33 reports that the voltage on the forced shutdown line of charger A sits below its valid band. What that means in practice depends on the logic, which no manufacturer publishes for this code.
s: Charger A never starts charging
Charging aborts when the car or harness is moved
Charging system warning message
c: Shutdown line chafed through and shorted to ground
Broken wire or backed-out pin in the shutdown circuit
Moisture or corrosion in the charger signal connector
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low

P2E34.d: P2E34 is set when the forced shutdown line of charger A reads above its permitted voltage. The usual cause is contact with a battery-fed or switched 12 V wire in the same harness, or an internal leak inside the charger or the commanding module.
s: Charger A disabled, plug-in charging not possible or slower
Charging system warning message
c: Shutdown line shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Internal leakage in charger A or the commanding module
Incorrect wiring after a previous harness repair

P2E35.d: P2E35 covers the enable line of charger B, the hardwired 12 V signal that wakes the charger or allows it to work, and reports a general circuit fault, usually an open. No manufacturer documents P2E35 publicly.
s: Charger B does not wake when the cable is plugged in
Charging slower than usual or not at all
Charging system warning message
c: Broken enable wire or backed-out terminal
Signal connector at charger B not fully latched
Failed enable driver in the commanding module

P2E36.d: P2E36 means the enable signal to charger B is pulled under the level its commanded state allows, most often by a short to ground or by a driver stage that cannot pull the line up. No manufacturer documents P2E36 publicly.
s: Charger B stays off whenever charging is requested
Lower charging power or no charging
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the charger B signal connector
Damaged high-side driver in the commanding module

P2E37.d: P2E37 is stored when the enable line of charger B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows, typically because it touches a powered wire or the driver in the commanding module is stuck on. No manufacturer documents P2E37 publicly.
s: 12 V battery discharged after standing
Charger B fan or pump runs with nothing plugged in
Charging via charger B disabled
c: Enable wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Enable driver in the commanding module stuck on
Internal leakage in the charger B input circuit

P2E38.d: P2E38 flags an enable circuit of charger B that is electrically sound, while the charger or its partner modules do not react to it as expected. No manufacturer documents P2E38 publicly.
s: Charging begins only after a long delay or not at all
Fault appears only on some charging sessions
c: Software mismatch between charger B and battery control module
Battery control module not waking or starting too slowly
Enable level marginal due to contact resistance

P2E39.d: P2E39 concerns the high-voltage fuse in the branch between the traction battery and charger B. Battery management units usually judge such fuses by comparing the voltage behind the fuse with the pack voltage; Volvo's technical journal TJ 37376 on BECM codes P0A9500 and P0E2F00 has technicians read exactly those values at the fuse outputs.
s: Charging through charger B no longer possible
Electrical system or high-voltage warning
c: Fuse opened by an internal short in charger B
Spurious entry from battery management software
Faulty voltage sensing behind the fuse

P2E3A.d: P2E3A says the high-voltage output of charger B does not follow its target, typically in the constant-voltage phase near the end of a charge, without being clearly too low. No manufacturer documents P2E3A publicly.
s: Battery does not reach full charge
Charging stops early or takes longer
Charging system warning message
c: Degraded power stage or regulation inside charger B
Charger or battery module software needing an update

P2E3B.d: P2E3B is set when the high-voltage output of charger B stays below what the control unit expects while charging. No manufacturer documents P2E3B publicly.
s: MIL on and vehicle will not charge
Level 2 charging fails, wall box breaker may trip
c: Charger module software fault fixed by reprogramming
Failed power stage inside charger B
High resistance in the HV output connection

P2E3C.d: P2E3C means charger B does not deliver the high-voltage current it has been asked for. No manufacturer documents P2E3C publicly.
s: MIL after or during charging
Charging takes noticeably longer or aborts
Problem more frequent in cold weather
c: Control software or calibration of charger or hybrid module
Weak power stage inside charger B

P2E3D.d: P2E3D points to a short on the high-voltage output side of charger B. No manufacturer documents P2E3D publicly.
s: Charging blocked as soon as the cable is plugged in
High-voltage or charging system warning
c: Internal short in the charger B output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger B and battery
Leaking or stuck contactor path in the charging circuit

P2E3E.d: P2E3E is the charger B version of P2E32: the forced shutdown signal of the second charger is electrically in range but its behaviour is implausible. Examples are a shutdown request that the charger ignores, or a level that changes state without a matching command, so the control unit can no longer trust its hardwired off-switch for path B.
s: Charging slower than usual because charger B is locked out
Charging system warning message
c: Shutdown input stage inside charger B not responding correctly
Intermittent contact in the charger B shutdown line
Software issue in the module issuing the shutdown

P2E3F.d: P2E3F reports a forced shutdown signal at charger B that stays below its permitted voltage. No manufacturer documents P2E3F or the shutdown logic behind it publicly.
s: Charger B never takes part in charging
Reduced charging power or no charging
c: Shutdown line of charger B shorted to ground
Broken wire or loose pin in the signal plug
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low

P2E40.d: P2E40 means the forced shutdown signal of charger B reads above its valid band, typically from a short to a 12 V wire or a leak inside the charger or the module that drives it. No manufacturer documents P2E40 publicly.
s: Charging slower or impossible with charger B locked out
Charging system warning message
c: Shutdown line of charger B shorted to a 12 V wire
Internal leakage in charger B or the commanding module
Miswiring after a harness or charger repair

P2E41.d: P2E41 flags an electrical fault on the line over which the controller commands electronics coolant pump B, the second pump serving inverter, DC/DC converter and frequently the charger; the maker decides which pump is B. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E41.
s: Hybrid or electric drive warning and MIL
Pump B does not run, electronics loop warms up faster
Reduced drive power or interrupted charging under high load
c: Broken or disconnected control wire between module and pump B
Corroded or pushed-back pins at the pump connector
Pump B electronics no longer load the command line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P2E42.d: P2E42 is the functional verdict on electronics coolant pump B: the circuits test fine, yet the controller concludes the pump is not doing its job. Two ways of reaching that verdict are documented for pump A.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Higher inverter or charger temperatures than usual
Power reduction or slower charging in hot conditions
c: Air pocket after service or slow coolant loss
Worn pump B delivering too little flow
Debris, kinked hose or clogged cold plate in the loop

P2E43.d: P2E43 means the command signal of electronics coolant pump B sits too low, typically because the line has contact with ground or the output stage cannot drive it up. On PWM-controlled pumps this usually stops the pump outright.
s: Pump B stops, electronics coolant heats up
MIL with hybrid or drive system message
Limited power or charging rate under load
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector
Shorted input stage inside pump B
Output stage of the module stuck low

P2E44.d: P2E44 is the opposite fault: the command line of electronics coolant pump B reads higher than its commanded state allows, mostly because it touches a battery-fed wire or the driver can no longer pull it down. Many PWM pumps react to a permanently high input with an emergency mode; Pierburg's interface runs the pump at about 95 % speed for a duty cycle of 98 to 100 %.
s: MIL with hybrid system message
Pump B runs continuously at high speed, audible hum
Pump does not respond to commanded speed changes
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Module output stage unable to pull the line low
Moisture linking supply and signal pins in the connector

P2E45.d: Some designs switch electronics coolant pump B on through a separate enable line or a relay, independent of the speed command; P2E45 reports a fault in that path. GM's 2018 hybrid tables show the scheme for pump A: with the enable output active, more than 0.6 A on the line counts as a short to ground (P1F44); with it inactive, more than 35 µA or a line voltage under 4.5 V counts as a short to voltage (P1F45), each af
s: Pump B never starts although commanded
MIL and hybrid or charging warning
Power or charging limited as electronics heat up
c: Enable wire open or shorted between module and pump
Pump relay or its fuse failed, where the design uses one
Faulty enable output in the controlling module

P2E46.d: P2E46 is the dry-run report of electronics coolant pump B: faster than commanded at lower current, the signature of air at the impeller. Porsche describes such self-monitoring on the traction-battery pump of the 2018 Panamera plug-in hybrid (code P0C4A00 there).
s: Coolant warning message and MIL
Pump starts briefly, then stops again
Gurgling noise or falling level in the electronics reservoir
c: Low coolant level from a leaking hose, joint or component
Air left in the loop after service without vacuum fill
Pump B damaged by earlier dry running

P2E47.d: P2E47 is set when electronics coolant pump B keeps turning but clearly slower than requested. GM's 2018 hybrid tables describe the check for pump A (P19FC): the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay within a calibrated band once the pump has run for 5 s at 11 to 90 % duty, otherwise a Type B fault results.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electronics temperatures rise during long drives or fast charging
Occasional power limitation
c: Stiff bearing or worn pump B
Deposits or debris slowing the impeller
Voltage drop on pump supply or ground under load
Incorrect or aged coolant, too viscous when cold

P2E48.d: With P2E48 the controller sees electronics coolant pump B turning faster than commanded, without the separate dry-run test (P2E46) having fired. The usual reason is lost load, since a centrifugal pump accelerates when its impeller gets less liquid, whether from a low level, a collapsed suction hose, partial air or an impeller slipping on its shaft.
s: MIL, sometimes with a coolant level warning
Louder pump noise than usual
Rising electronics temperatures and power limits
c: Low level or residual air in the electronics loop
Collapsed or kinked hose on the pump inlet side
Impeller slipping on the pump shaft
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2E49.d: P2E49 reports that electronics coolant pump B is powered and commanded, but its rotor does not turn or comes to a standstill. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV shows such a test for its electric water pump: with more than 9 V supply the PHEV-ECU sets P10D9 once the reported speed stays under 100 rpm for 0.5 s, against about 500 rpm when healthy.
s: MIL and hybrid or drive system warning
Rapid temperature rise in inverter or charger
Strong power reduction or charging stops
c: Seized bearing or failed pump B motor
Debris or sealant residue jamming the impeller
Frozen coolant due to insufficient antifreeze
Supply or ground lost under load

P2E4A.d: P2E4A is the general electrical fault of a third temperature measuring point in the charging inlet, logged when the module sees a defective circuit but does not sort it into low, high or implausible. Unlike sensors A and B, the C row has no intermittent code of its own.
s: Charging refused or only possible at reduced power
Charging system warning in the cluster or the app
Charge indicator at the inlet signals a fault
c: Sensor lead or crimp between inlet and evaluating module broken
Low-voltage connector of the inlet harness loose or corroded
Temperature element C (or one element of a PTC chain) failed inside the inlet
Measuring input in the charger or charge control module defective

P2E4B.d: P2E4B concerns a sensor C value that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation, for instance a reading that ignores a heavy charge current, departs from the other inlet sensors or jumps without cause. CARB wants such rationality faults kept under their own code, apart from codes for wiring faults and values beyond the limits.
s: Charging stops or starts at reduced power, often at busy public stations
Fault does not reappear until the car has been driven for a while
Charging warning message
c: Worn or widened terminals in the charging station plug heating the contact unevenly
Sensor no longer in good thermal contact with its pin
Plausibility logic in the charging software too strict, update available
Temperature element drifted from its characteristic curve

P2E4C.d: P2E4C says the voltage on the sensor C input has fallen under its lower limit. Low is about the signal; the temperature it implies depends on the element.
s: Charging blocked at once or ended shortly after start
Charging system warning
Fault may follow rain or a car wash
c: Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion bridging the sensor terminals in the inlet or its connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective

P2E4D.d: P2E4D is stored when the sensor C input rises above its upper limit. In a pull-up circuit that is the signature of an open loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage.
s: Charging does not start or stops immediately
Charging system warning
Displayed inlet temperature stuck at an extreme value
c: Sensor C loop open, for example a broken wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element C or one link of a PTC chain open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective

P2E4E.d: P2E4E is no sensor fault: measuring point C works, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is cut back or ended. For orientation, a DOE laboratory report from August 2025 compares the IEC 62196-1 ceiling, 90 °C when the air is at 40 °C, with the fixed 100 °C of SAE J3400.
s: Charging slows down or stops partway through
Charge indicator at the inlet flashes a fault or reduced-power state
Discoloured or heat-marked pins at the plug or inlet
c: Worn, widened or dirty pins in the station plug or the vehicle inlet
Charging cable with thin conductors heating up at high current (Porsche)
Long high-current session in strong heat or direct sun
Temperature logic in the charging software, update available

P2E4F.d: P2E4F is the general circuit fault of the fourth inlet temperature sensor, used when the wiring is clearly wrong but not classed as low, high or implausible; the D row has no intermittent code either. Ford is the one maker whose public papers show a sensor D in use: SSM 55080 names P2E53, the overheating verdict for point D, stored in the secondary OBD module (SOBDM) of the Mustang Mach-E, E-Transit and F-150 Lightni
s: DC fast charging refused or limited
Charging warning in the cluster
Fault may only show with a warm or cold inlet
c: Low-voltage connector between inlet harness and evaluating module loose (smart for sensor A)
Sensor D wiring chafed or broken
Temperature element D failed (normally replaced with the inlet)
Measuring input in the SOBDM or charger defective

P2E50.d: P2E50 flags sensor D for delivering a believable voltage that the logic still rejects. A module can test this in several ways: compare D with a sensor on a contact that carries the same current, check whether it warms as expected under load, or look for steps no metal pin could make.
s: DC fast charging limited or ended early
AC charging may still work
Charging warning message
c: Sensor D has lost good thermal contact with its pin
One contact heating far more than its partner due to wear or dirt
Plausibility thresholds in the module software, update available

P2E51.d: P2E51 reports a sensor D voltage below the valid band. TE Connectivity lists thermistors, thermocouples and resistance temperature detectors as candidate elements for inlet sensing (US10960781), and the patent also explains the stakes: contact resistance heats the inlet at high current and could melt parts or start a fire if nobody watches.
s: DC fast charging refused
Charging warning message
Inlet temperature reading implausible in live data
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective

P2E52.d: P2E52 is the mirror case of P2E51: the sensor D input sits above its valid band, usually because of an interrupted sensor lead, a connector that has backed out, or a short to a supply line. Volex quotes for its NACS inlet NTC thermistors with an operating range of -40 to +125 °C; an open NTC loop looks like a contact colder than that range, which hides any real heating.
s: DC fast charging does not start or stops at once
Charging warning message
Inlet temperature reading fixed at an extreme value
c: Sensor D lead broken or connector backed out
Signal wire shorted to a supply line
Temperature element D open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective

P2E53.d: P2E53 means measuring point D in the charging inlet reports a contact that is too hot, and charging is throttled or halted. Ford documents this exact code in SSM 55080: on Mustang Mach-E built up to 25 June 2023, E-Transit 2022-2025 and F-150 Lightning 2022-2023, DC fast charging can stop with P2E53:27 and/or P0EEE:27 in the SOBDM.
s: DC fast charging stops at level 3 stations
AC charging at home or level 2 still works
Charging power reduced during fast charging
c: SOBDM software misjudging DC fast-charge heating (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn or contaminated DC pins in the station plug or the inlet
Very high charging current in hot weather
Heat-damaged inlet contacts needing a new charge port

P2E54.d: P2E54 is the general circuit fault of a third exhaust pressure sensor, C. Its position is set by the manufacturer; engines can carry several such sensors, as in a GE patent with one pressure sensor in each of two exhaust manifolds.
s: MIL on
Reduced power if boost or EGR control falls back to substitute values
Other exhaust or EGR monitors may not run
c: Exhaust pressure sensor C failed internally
Wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat or chafing
Corroded or loose connector at sensor C

P2E55.d: P2E55 is the plausibility test of exhaust pressure sensor C: the voltage is in range, but the pressure does not suit the operating state. CARB wants such rationality faults stored apart from circuit faults.
s: MIL, often without noticeable driveability change
Particulate filter or EGR codes alongside
Reduced power if the pressure is really too high
c: Real back pressure from a clogged particulate filter or catalyst
Sooted or cracked sensing tube to sensor C
Sensor C offset drifted or stuck mid-range
Exhaust leak near the measuring point

P2E56.d: P2E56 means the signal of exhaust pressure sensor C stays under the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Analogue exhaust pressure sensors return a share of their 5 V reference; Ford's petrol transfer function for sensor A puts 49 kPa at 0.3 V and flags anything under 0.21 V for 5 s, while its 2023 diesels use 0.1 V for 2 s.
s: MIL on
Possible loss of power from substitute values
Further low codes of sensors sharing the reference
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor

P2E57.d: P2E57 reports a signal from exhaust pressure sensor C above the plausible ceiling. For sensor A Ford sets that ceiling at 4.80 V, on petrol engines checked while the EGR monitor runs and with 5 s to fail, on 2023 diesels with 2 s; in Ford's petrol transfer function 4.7 V already equals about 378 kPa.
s: MIL on
Boost or EGR control in substitute mode, possibly less power
c: Open ground circuit of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open signal wire pulled high by the module input

P2E58.d: P2E58 is the collective misfire code for running on the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG: misfires are counted while gas is burned, but no single cylinder can be blamed, or several each carry a large share. CARB treats a bi-fuel car as alternate-fueled only while it runs on gas and asks for the same misfire monitor as on petrol; EPA likewise requires converters to keep OBD working on the conversion fuel.
s: Rough running or jerking only while the engine runs on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle switches back to petrol on its own
Check engine light on or flashing, gas-mode indicator may flash
c: Gas pressure regulator or LPG vaporiser iced up or not heated enough (low coolant flow, moisture in the gas)
Too little gas pressure at the rail – clogged gas filter, nearly empty tank or weak regulator
Worn plugs or weak coils on several cylinders that cope with petrol but not with the harder-to-ignite gas mixture
Lean gas mixture from an intake air leak or wrong gas-system calibration

P2E59.d: P2E59 means that, while the engine is burning its gaseous fuel, the misfire monitor puts the dropouts on cylinder 1; CARB allows a single-cylinder code once more than 90 % of counted misfires fall on one cylinder. In most numbering schemes cylinder 1 is the frontmost.
s: Rough idle on gas that disappears in petrol mode
Stumble at the moment the system changes over to gas
Check engine light, possibly flashing under load
c: Sticking or leaking gas injector on cylinder 1
Cracked injector hose or loose nozzle in the intake port of cylinder 1
Weak coil or worn plug on cylinder 1 that fails only under gas
Fault in the fuel changeover module or its programming (misfire only at the switch from petrol to gas)

P2E5A.d: P2E5A says cylinder 2 is the one losing combustion while the engine is supplied with alternative fuel; P0302 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Uneven running on gas, normal on petrol
Higher gas consumption and loss of power
Check engine light
c: Gas injector on cylinder 2 gummed or sluggish from compressor oil in the gas
Injector harness of the conversion routed crosswise, so cylinder 2 receives another cylinder's pulse
Injection nozzle of cylinder 2 not properly seated in the manifold port
Coil or plug on cylinder 2 too weak for gas operation

P2E5B.d: P2E5B flags misfire on cylinder 3 during operation on CNG or LPG; on petrol the matching code is P0303. No manufacturer publishes P2E5B.
s: Misfire on gas that slowly gets worse, later also on petrol
Low compression on cylinder 3, sometimes a ticking valve noise
Check engine light
c: Valve seat recession on cylinder 3 from dry gas operation, valve no longer seals
Worn plug or failing coil on cylinder 3
Retrofit gas conversion on an engine without hardened valves and seats

P2E5C.d: P2E5C is stored when the misfire counter blames cylinder 4 while gas is being burned; in petrol mode the code would be P0304. No manufacturer documents P2E5C publicly, and Deutz's fault list for its eControls LPG, CNG and bi-fuel engines reports such events with the ordinary P0301 to P0304.
s: Misfire mainly under load or acceleration on gas
Engine runs cleanly after switching to petrol
Check engine light, flashing during heavy misfire
c: Spark plug on cylinder 4 worn or unsuited for gas (gap too wide, wrong heat range)
Coil or plug boot on cylinder 4 breaking down under the higher firing voltage
Gas injector on cylinder 4 sticking or delivering too little

P2E5D.d: P2E5D assigns gas-mode misfire to cylinder 5, which exists only on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the 3.6-litre V6 in GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel, V8 trucks or inline-six gas engines in buses. P0305 is the petrol equivalent.
s: Vibration and power loss on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle drops back to petrol
Check engine light
c: Spark plug on cylinder 5 past its change interval or damaged when handled
Low-pressure oil separator/filter not serviced, oil reaches the gas injector of cylinder 5
Cracked coil extension or boot on cylinder 5 (heavy-duty gas engines)

P2E5E.d: P2E5E names cylinder 6 as the misfiring one while the engine runs on alternative fuel; P0306 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents the code openly.
s: Misfire or rough running shortly after a hot restart
Long cranking time when the engine is warm
Check engine light
c: Gas or liquid-propane injector on cylinder 6 sticking or leaking
Propane vapour in the liquid-injection rail (hot restart, low rail or tank pressure)
Plug or coil on cylinder 6 failing under gas
Low tank pressure in cold weather or nearly empty tank

P2E5F.d: P2E5F puts alternative-fuel misfire on cylinder 7, so it concerns eight-cylinder engines, for instance GM's Vortec 6.0 V8 in the bi-fuel Silverado/Sierra or the dedicated CNG and LPG Express/Savana vans that GM lists in its gaseous-fuel overview bulletin. P0307 is the petrol counterpart.
s: Rough running on gas, smooth on petrol
Gas-mode indicator flashing or automatic return to petrol
Check engine light
c: Gas injector on cylinder 7 faulty or sticking
Leaking injector sleeve or loose nozzle at cylinder 7's intake runner
Conversion injector harness damaged or misrouted near the rear of the engine
Coil or plug on cylinder 7 too weak for gas

P2E60.d: P2E60 is the last cylinder-specific code of the alternative-fuel misfire group and points to cylinder 8; the next code, P2E61, covers misfire with low fuel. Petrol twin: P0308.
s: Misfire on gas, possibly with lean codes on one bank
Engine shakes at idle on gas
Check engine light
c: Deposits from compressor oil in the gas injector serving cylinder 8
Coil or plug on cylinder 8, often hard to reach at the rear of the engine
Uneven gas split between the two rails starving the bank with cylinder 8 (older bi-fuel systems)
Valve seat wear on cylinder 8 after long gas operation

P2E61.d: P2E61 records misfire that occurs while the engine burns its gaseous fuel and that fuel is almost used up. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: Stumbling or power loss on gas when the gas gauge is near empty
Vehicle changes over to petrol on its own
Check engine light on
c: Gas tank close to empty, so the regulator can no longer hold rail pressure
Tank pressure or level signal reads too high, so the system stays on gas too long
Restriction in the gas line (clogged filter, ice) that only shows when tank pressure is low
Worn plugs or coils that cannot ignite the leaner gas mixture near empty

P2E62.d: Coolant bypass valve E is the fifth electrically driven coolant valve in the SAE lettering; which coolant path it controls (heater, radiator, transmission, block) is up to the carmaker. P2E62 says the engine computer sees an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit.
s: Check engine light or service message
Heating, warm-up or cooling behaves differently, depending on what valve E controls
Valve stays in its de-energised default position
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the valve
Broken wire in the drive or supply line
Open winding in the valve actuator motor or solenoid
ECM software fault or defective output stage

P2E63.d: P2E63 flags a drive line for coolant bypass valve E whose voltage is lower than the commanded state allows, typically a grounded wire or a heavy leakage path to ground in the harness or the actuator. No carmaker documents valve E publicly.
s: Check engine light, sometimes a maintenance message
Valve does not move or stays in its default position
Slower warm-up or changed heater output
c: Chafed drive wire touching engine ground
Internal short in the valve actuator, often after coolant got into it
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2E64.d: P2E64 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of coolant bypass valve E carries more voltage than expected, usually because it touches a supply wire, or the load has gone open in a way the output stage reads as high. Valve E itself appears in no public manufacturer document.
s: Check engine light
Valve is not driven and stays in its de-energised position
Possible change in heater output or warm-up time
c: Drive wire chafed through and touching a battery-voltage wire
Moisture or coolant in the connector creating a path to supply voltage
Open actuator winding that the output stage reads as high voltage
Defective output stage in the engine control module

P2E65.d: P2E65 is a functional fault: the electrics of valve E are fine, but the valve remains open although it was told to close. The official title is written Stuck/Open, though it means stuck open, the partner of P2E67.
s: Engine and cabin heat take longer to come up
Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel use on short trips
c: Valve body jammed open by deposits or worn seals
Broken gear or weak actuator that cannot drive the valve closed
Position sensor or its wiring reporting an open valve that is actually closed
Chafed engine harness disturbing drive or feedback signals

P2E66.d: P2E66 is the broad plausibility code for valve E: the valve moves, but not to the right place, not fast enough, or its feedback does not match the command, without a clear stuck-open or stuck-closed verdict. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly.
s: Check engine light, sometimes a coolant or maintenance message
Uneven heater output or warm-up
Possible fallback to a fixed valve position
c: Cracked or worn gear inside the valve actuator
Valve sluggish from deposits, degraded coolant or worn seals
Position sensor drifting or lost end-stop learn values
Low supply voltage slowing the actuator

P2E67.d: P2E67 means valve E stays shut although the control asked it to open. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly.
s: Check engine light
Little or no heat from the heater, or rising engine temperature, depending on the circuit
Possible reduced engine power to protect the engine
c: Valve jammed closed by deposits, debris or swollen seals
Actuator motor or gearing unable to open the valve
Position feedback stuck at the closed value
Wrong coolant or trapped air after service upsetting the temperature-based check

P2E68.d: P2E68 is a fuel trim fault that is judged only while cylinders are shut off: in that mode bank 1 needs more fuel correction than allowed. GM uses it on its 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 (LTA, table 19OBDG07): the engine learns a separate multiplicative long-term trim for deactivation mode, and the code sets when that factor for bank 1 rises above 1.23 and has been steady for at least 10 s; Type B, MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Slight shake or surge at light cruise when cylinders are shut off
Cylinder deactivation may be used less often
c: Restricted injector on one of the cylinders that keep firing on bank 1
Unmetered air entering bank 1 (intake leak, seal, PCV)
Deactivating rocker or lifter on bank 1 not holding the valves shut, pumping air into the exhaust
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased rich

P2E69.d: P2E69 is the rich mirror of P2E68: with cylinders deactivated, bank 1 has to pull fuel out beyond the permitted range. In GM's 19OBDG07 tables for the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 the separate long-term trim factor learned for deactivation mode must drop below 0.77 and stay steady; it shares the enable logic of P2E68 and is Type B, MIL on the second trip.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel use, possible fuel smell
Rough running in deactivation mode
c: A cylinder that should be off still breathing, so measured airflow and fuel delivery are too high
Leaking or dribbling direct injector on bank 1
Fuel vapour from diluted oil or a stuck-open purge valve
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased lean

P2E6A.d: P2E6A applies the lean test to bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1. GM sets it on the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 of the 2019 table 19OBDG07 when the trim factor learned for deactivation mode on bank 2 exceeds 1.23 while stable; Type B.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Hesitation at light load in deactivation mode
Often no noticeable change in normal driving
c: Weak injector on cylinder 4 or 6, which carry bank 2 in deactivation mode
Bank 2 high-pressure fuel pump delivering too little
Deactivating rocker on bank 2 letting air pass into the exhaust
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor

P2E6B.d: P2E6B closes the set: bank 2 runs rich while cylinders are switched off. GM's 19OBDG07 tables (4.2-litre twin-turbo V8, LTA) fail the test when bank 2's deactivation-mode trim factor falls below 0.77 and has settled; Type B, two trips, same enable conditions as the other three codes.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel consumption on the highway
Possible sooty tailpipe on bank 2 side
c: Leaking injector on bank 2, including one on a cylinder that should be shut off
Deactivation rocker or its oil-control solenoid not switching on one cylinder
Excess purge vapour or fuel-diluted engine oil
Bank 2 oxygen sensor reading biased lean

P2E6C.d: P2E6C means the cells of high-voltage pack A have become thicker than the battery controller tolerates: the cells are swelling. A healthy cell only breathes a little while charging; GE and University of Michigan measured about 0.1 mm, 1 % of its thickness, on the Sanyo cell of Ford's Fusion HEV pack.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, often with reduced power
Vehicle may not switch to READY because the main contactors stay open
Charging blocked or limited
c: Aged cells in pack A that have grown permanently thicker
Gas build-up in cells after overcharging or overheating
Module clamping or end plates loosened, so cells can expand further

P2E6D.d: P2E6D says the signal from the cell thickness sensor of pack A sits above the range the controller accepts as a real reading. The code describes the voltage, not swollen cells.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Power or charging limited as a precaution
In some designs the vehicle will not go to READY
c: Open signal or ground wire, unplugged or corroded connector inside pack A
Signal wire chafed against a supply or reference line
Thickness or pressure sensing element itself failed open

P2E6E.d: P2E6E is the low-side counterpart to P2E6D: the thickness or swelling sensor of pack A delivers less signal than any intact circuit should, typically from a short to ground, a missing supply or a dead sensor amplifier. No manufacturer documents P2E6E publicly.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Reduced power or limited charging
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or to the module housing
Sensor supply or amplifier supply missing
Sensing element or its amplifier failed
Moisture or coolant in a connector inside the pack creating a leakage path

P2E6F.d: P2E6F covers a thickness sensor in pack A whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave as the controller expects. Cell thickness is not static: it rises and falls with state of charge, which is why Bosch and Samsung SDI propose using the swelling force of the winding to estimate charge and health, and a graphene film sensor studied at Warwick tracked charge level from expansion alone.
s: Warning light without noticeable driving change at first
Charging or power may be restricted later
c: Sensor loosened, shifted or no longer bonded to the cell or end plate
Sensor drifting with age or temperature
Contact resistance in connectors distorting the reading
Missing calibration or relearn after module replacement

P2E70.d: P2E70 is the swelling code for a second high-voltage pack, B, in vehicles that carry two; which pack is A and which B is set by the maker. The controller judges that cells in pack B have grown too thick.
s: Hybrid or EV warning with power reduction
Reduced range or charging blocked
Vehicle may refuse READY
c: Cells in pack B aged and permanently thicker
Gas generation after overcharge, deep discharge or heat
Poor cooling of pack B accelerating cell degradation

P2E71.d: P2E71 flags the thickness sensor circuit of pack B as reading too high. Not every swelling detector is analog: LG's module patent uses a panel that slides along a ramp until it touches a contact sensor, and a Lithium Energy and Power patent fits cells with insulated contact elements that close under pressure.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Possibly limited power or charging
c: Sensor connector in pack B not fully seated after battery work
Broken signal or ground wire to the sensor
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage

P2E72.d: P2E72 means the pack B thickness sensor reports a signal below its valid floor. On a bridge-type strain gauge, the output is a small fraction of the excitation voltage that grows with strain, so losing that excitation or shorting a bridge leg to ground pulls the reading towards zero.
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Power or charging may be reduced as a precaution
c: Signal line or sensor shorted to ground inside pack B
Sensor excitation or reference supply lost
Fault in the measuring circuit of the battery monitoring module

P2E73.d: P2E73 indicates that the thickness sensor of pack B delivers values within range that the controller cannot reconcile with what it otherwise knows about the pack. Free expansion of a healthy cell is small, about 1 % of its thickness on the Ford Fusion HEV cell measured by GE, so a sensor must resolve fractions of a millimetre; GE's thin eddy-current coils between cells covered 0 to 2 mm.
s: Warning light, often with no other complaint
Battery controller may limit power or charging rate
c: Sensor mounting or gap changed, for example after module work
Sensor drift or degraded sensing element
Plausibility limits in the battery controller software too tight

P2E74.d: P2E74 covers any circuit fault of coolant temperature sensor D, the fourth such sensor a maker can fit to the battery's liquid cooling. Battery controllers typically watch coolant at the pack inlet and outlet; GM's Volt and ELR tables use sensor A for the inlet and B for the outlet.
s: Hybrid system or check engine light
Battery cooling or heating not working as intended
Reduced electric power or charging rate
c: Damaged wire, loose connector or corroded terminal at sensor D
Fault on the shared 5 V reference circuit of the battery controller

P2E75.d: P2E75 means battery coolant sensor D gives a reading that is electrically fine yet does not match the other temperatures in the loop. No manufacturer documents P2E75 publicly.
s: Warning light, frequently with no other symptom
Less effective battery cooling or heating
c: Sensor D drifting or responding slowly
Plausibility logic in controller software too strict (update available)
Air pocket or poor coolant flow around the sensor

P2E76.d: P2E76 reports that the voltage on battery coolant sensor D has dropped below its lower limit. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, a low voltage stands for very hot coolant, and a grounded signal wire or a sensor with an internal short produces exactly that picture.
s: Hybrid or check engine warning
Cooling may run at full effort or power may be cut back
c: Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
Sensor D shorted internally, for example after coolant entered it
Actual overheating of the battery coolant loop

P2E77.d: P2E77 is set when the signal of battery coolant sensor D rises to or near the reference voltage. In a pull-up NTC circuit that is the signature of an open: a disconnected plug, a broken wire, a spread pin or a sensor element that has gone open, and the controller then sees a coolant temperature colder than physically plausible.
s: Hybrid or check engine warning
Battery heating may switch on needlessly or behave oddly in winter
c: Sensor D connector unplugged or not latched after cooling system work
Broken wire or spread terminal in the sensor D circuit

P2E78.d: P2E78 stands for a coolant temperature from sensor D that jumps around, mostly without leaving the electrical limits. A liquid loop changes temperature slowly, so fast swings point to a loose contact rather than to the coolant.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Coolant temperature in live data jumping
c: Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor D connector
Harness rubbing through near moving or vibrating parts

P2E79.d: P2E79 is the functional verdict on a third pump in the coolant loop of the traction electronics: command and wiring look healthy, yet the pump does not move coolant the way the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P2E79 or says which pump it calls C.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp, possibly MIL
Drive power or charging rate limited because electronics run warm
Gurgling or whirring noise from the electronics coolant loop
c: Air trapped in the electronics coolant loop after service or a leak
Pump C worn or impeller fouled, delivering too little flow
Kinked hose or clogged cooler passages in the loop
Control software misjudging pump function (update available)

P2E7A.d: P2E7A means the third electronics coolant pump spins faster than the speed it was given. A centrifugal pump that draws air instead of liquid loses its load and races, so a low coolant level, a leak or a poorly bled loop come first, a slipping impeller or false speed feedback later.
s: Coolant or hybrid system warning, possibly MIL
Coolant reservoir level dropping, traces of leakage
Pump runs loud or churns; power or charging may be reduced
c: Coolant level low or air pocket at the pump inlet
Leak or defective seal in the electronics coolant loop
Impeller loose on its shaft or broken
Faulty speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2E7B.d: P2E7B is the general circuit fault of the measuring element for the DC field current in the rotor of drive motor A. It exists only in electrically excited synchronous motors, whose rotor field comes from a winding, as in Renault's Megane E-Tech, Nissan's Ariya and BMW's fifth-generation eDrive.
s: Electric drive warning lamp and MIL
Noticeably reduced power or no drive from motor A
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode
c: Supply or reference of the excitation current sensor lost
Open or corroded connection between sensor and motor controller
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed
Measuring input inside the inverter or motor controller defective

P2E7C.d: P2E7C covers the second internal temperature sensor in the control electronics of an electric A/C compressor. Their inverter sits on the housing: a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries patent places a sensor next to the power switches, Denso measures at the switches and at the motor stator, and TI's compressor inverter reference feeds IGBT temperature back for overheat protection.
s: A/C cools weakly or switches off
On plug-in hybrids and EVs, battery cooling and fast charging may be limited
Warning message on the climate display; MIL depends on the manufacturer
c: Sensor B or its circuit on the compressor control board defective
Compressor controller fails to evaluate or transmit the value
Unstable 12 V supply, ground or data link to the compressor

P2E7D.d: P2E7D is the plausibility check for internal temperature sensor B of the electric A/C compressor controller: the reading is electrically in range yet conflicts with other temperatures. The test runs after a long rest, when all sensors should read alike.
s: Usually no noticeable effect at first; fault stored after a cold start
Compressor may derate early or shut off on a wrong temperature
MIL on some vehicles after two drive cycles
c: Sensor B drifted or poorly coupled to its measuring point
Comparison value wrong, e.g. outside air or second internal sensor faulty
Compressor still warm from recent use or preconditioning when the test ran

P2E7E.d: P2E7E reports that internal temperature sensor B of the A/C compressor controller delivers a signal above its valid range. Most sensors of this kind produce a voltage that falls as temperature rises; TI's compressor inverter reference uses such an analog part, so a high signal stands for an impossibly cold reading.
s: Compressor runs restricted or not at all
Cabin and, where present, battery cooling weaker
MIL possible after two drive cycles depending on manufacturer
c: Sensor B path open, e.g. cracked solder joint on the board
Reference or ground of the measuring circuit lost inside the module
Analog input of the compressor controller defective

P2E7F.d: P2E7F is the low-signal counterpart: sensor B inside the compressor control module reports a value below its valid band, which for a sensor with falling output means an impossibly hot reading. GM's comparable code on the compressor IGBT sensor is P0D78: the 2011 Volt fails above 274 °C, the 2018 and 2019 tables above 150 °C, with the compressor detecting the condition itself and passing it on over GMLAN, Type B.
s: Compressor derates or shuts down for overheat protection
Air conditioning blows warm, battery cooling may be limited
MIL possible after two drive cycles depending on manufacturer
c: Short circuit in the sensor B path on the control board
Power stage genuinely overheating, e.g. low refrigerant charge
Measuring circuit of the compressor controller defective

P2E80.d: With P2E80 the controller sees the reading of sensor B, a second internal thermometer in the compressor electronics, flicker: values leap or vanish for an instant and then look normal again. Set criteria for P2E80 are not published by any manufacturer.
s: A/C cuts out and recovers sporadically
Fault may be stored without any noticeable effect
c: Loose contact or cold solder joint in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference from the inverter switching on the measuring line
Fluctuating 12 V supply or ground of the compressor controller

P2E81.d: P2E81 is the cold-start version of P26C2 for valve D, which GM uses as the block rotary valve between two mechanical end stops. Its 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) count a failure when commanded and measured position differ by more than 5° while raw feedback stays below 50°, i.e.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine temperature rising faster or unevenly after a cold start
Usually no driveability change
c: Block rotary valve stuck on the closed side (deposits, wear)
Valve actuator too weak to turn the valve when coolant is cold and thick
Chafed or corroded harness to the valve actuator
Invalid end-stop learn values after repair or battery disconnect

P2E82.d: P2E82 flags an electric main coolant pump that spins faster than requested while the cold-start warm-up strategy runs. GM's 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) subtract reported from requested speed, filter the result and fail the test when it falls below −200 rpm in 8 of 10 seconds; Type B, MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Gurgling noises or weak heater output
Rising engine temperature if coolant is missing
c: Low coolant level or air trapped after service, so the impeller runs dry
Impeller loose or damaged, so the motor turns without load
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal
Flow path blocked by a stuck valve, changing the pump load

P2E83.d: P2E83 covers a fuel rail pressure check that runs once the engine is shut down: the residual pressure in the rail falls too fast, stays too high or behaves implausibly. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: Check engine light
Long cranking or rough start after the car has stood
Possible fuel smell or smoke right after starting
c: Injector leaking into the cylinder, so rail pressure decays too quickly
Leaking pump check valve or pressure relief valve
Rail pressure sensor with offset or drift, implausible at rest
Pressure rising after shutdown from heat soak with no way to relieve it

P2E84.d: P2E84 questions the plausibility of the grid voltage that charger B reads at its input: the sensor answers within its electrical limits, yet the figure does not suit the moment, such as a voltage with no supply connected or a value that contradicts other readings. No manufacturer documents P2E84 publicly.
s: AC charging does not start or stops after a short time
DC fast charging still works normally
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster or app
c: Voltage sensing inside charger B drifting or faulty
Corroded or loose AC contacts between charge inlet and charger B
Unstable or unusual supply from the charging station or house circuit

P2E85.d: P2E85 means the input voltage signal of charger B sits too low, so the car sees little or no grid voltage while it expects AC. GM uses the code on its battery-electric models, from the 2017 Bolt EV to the Lyriq, Hummer EV, Blazer, Equinox and Silverado EV and BrightDrop vans, under the wording input voltage sensor circuit low voltage.
s: Vehicle does not charge on a Level 1 or Level 2 AC charger
DC fast charging works without the adapter problem
Further charger codes such as P0D3F or P0F71 stored
c: DC-only NACS adapter used on an AC charger
Charging station or house circuit not delivering AC voltage
Open or high-resistance AC path between inlet and charger B
Sensing circuit inside charger B shorted to ground

P2E86.d: P2E86 flags an input voltage signal of charger B above the highest value the measurement can plausibly produce. Home sockets and AC stations stay far below that, so the fault normally lies in the sensing path or its signal line, rarely in the grid.
s: AC charging refused or ended immediately
Charging system warning in the cluster
Fault returns at once after clearing, even on a known good charger
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B faulty
Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Lost reference ground of the measurement

P2E87.d: P2E87 is the general fault of a second plug-detection circuit, B, whose job is to tell the vehicle that a connector is seated in an inlet. Under SAE J1772 this proximity pin is tied to earth through resistors and a switch in the latch button, so the car can lock out driving and wind down current before the plug comes out; CHAdeMO inlets have their own proximity contact for the same interlock.
s: No charging through the affected inlet
Plug not recognised or vehicle reports a cable while none is fitted
Vehicle may refuse to enter drive readiness
c: Damaged or corroded proximity contact in inlet B
Open or poorly seated connector between inlet B and the controller
Faulty charging cable or plug resistor
Evaluation circuit in the charger or control unit faulty

P2E88.d: P2E88 flags plug sensing on circuit B whose value is electrically valid but makes no sense, typically a voltage that falls between the defined steps for no plug, plug latched and release button pressed. Those steps come from fixed resistors: J1772 uses 150 Ω plus 330 Ω once the latch is opened, and IEC 62196 cables code their current rating with values from about 100 Ω to 1.5 kΩ, each read within a tolerance band.
s: Charging aborts or the current is limited unexpectedly
Plug status changes without anyone touching the connector
Fault appears only with certain cables
c: Worn or dirty proximity contact raising the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard coding resistor
Moisture in inlet B creating leakage paths
Control software judging the signal wrongly
